core: Working definition: classical conditioning is learning in which a neutral stimulus comes to trigger a response after being paired with a stimulus that already triggers it (learning by association)
Attribution of the discovery to Ivan Pavlov as history (Russian physiologist, 1849-1936, digestion research)
The five pairing terms: unconditioned stimulus, unconditioned response, neutral stimulus, conditioned stimulus, conditioned response
Acquisition as the pairing phase (repeated pairings, timing matters; taste-aversion exception)
Extinction: conditioned response fades when the conditioned stimulus appears without the unconditioned stimulus
Spontaneous recovery: an extinguished conditioned response returns after a pause
Honest note: Pavlov's dogs as the classic case; phobias and advertising as everyday echoes
Honest framing: classical conditioning as the brain's pattern matcher
supporting: Fear conditioning and its role in phobias (cues paired with panic/distress trigger anxiety on their own)
Advertising: products paired with athletes or scenes that already produce positive feelings inherit some of that feeling
Taste aversion as a special acquisition case (single pairing, hours-long interval)
Watson and Rayner's conditioned-fear work with Little Albert as attributed history (not detailed in the lesson)
outOfScope: Behaviorism as a school of thought and Watson's broader theory
Clinical treatment of phobias or anxiety (educational overview only)

claims.claim: Classical conditioning is a form of learning by association: a neutral stimulus comes to trigger a response after being repeatedly paired with a stimulus that already triggers that response, so the organism learns to anticipate events.

Ivan Pavlov (1849-1936), a Russian physiologist who won a Nobel Prize for his research on digestion, discovered the process: his dogs salivated to cues that predicted food, such as the sight of the food bowl, the sound of assistants' footsteps, and tones, lights, or touches he paired with food.
An unconditioned stimulus triggers a reflexive, unlearned response; the unconditioned response is that natural reaction (for example, food makes a dog salivate with no training).

A neutral stimulus does not elicit the response before conditioning; after repeated pairing with the unconditioned stimulus it becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers the response on its own, and that learned reaction is the conditioned response.

Acquisition is the initial period of learning during which the neutral stimulus and unconditioned stimulus are paired and the association forms; timing matters, with only a brief interval in most conditioning, though taste aversion can be learned from a single pairing even hours later.
Extinction is the decrease and eventual disappearance of the conditioned response when the conditioned stimulus is presented without the unconditioned stimulus.
Spontaneous recovery is the return of a previously extinguished conditioned response after a rest period or lapse in exposure to the conditioned stimulus.

Stimulus generalization is responding with the conditioned response to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus (the more similar, the stronger the response); stimulus discrimination is learning to respond differently to similar stimuli, reserving the response for the conditioned stimulus.

Classical conditioning underlies everyday fear: when a cue (such as a crowded bus or a specific place) has been paired with panic or distress, the cue alone can trigger anxiety; psychologists describe this as fear conditioning, and it plays a role in phobias.
Advertising uses the same association process: a product repeatedly paired with an athlete or scene that already produces positive feelings can come to produce those feelings itself.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How the defining relationship of classical conditioning is worded across sources.
positions: OpenStax Psychology 2e: a process by which we learn to associate stimuli and, consequently, to anticipate events.
Noba Project (Bouton): learning to associate neutral stimuli with psychologically significant events; the neutral stimulus becomes a signal for the significant event.
Some textbook glosses emphasize the response transfer (the neutral stimulus 'comes to trigger the same response').
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the pairing-based working definition required by the topic brief (a neutral stimulus comes to trigger a response through pairing), which is consistent with both sources; anticipation and signaling are presented as the function of the learned association, not as competing definitions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether extinction erases the learned association or merely suppresses it.
positions: Spontaneous recovery (and the renewal effect) shows the original association can reappear after a pause or context change, so extinction is not permanent erasure.
Some popular summaries describe extinction as 'unlearning' or 'forgetting' the response.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that extinction weakens and removes the current response while spontaneous recovery shows the old pattern was suppressed rather than destroyed; no claim of permanent erasure is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Watson and Rayner's Little Albert experiment is ethically fraught by modern standards and its details are contested.
positions: OpenStax describes it as a historical demonstration that emotions could become conditioned responses.
Modern research-ethics standards would not permit the procedure.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson mentions conditioned fear as a phenomenon verified by the two Tier A sources and does not detail the Little Albert experiment; the historical Pavlov work is the only named experimental case, attributed as history.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's definition ('A foundational Psychology concept covered in this lesson') is circular and unsupported by any source.
The draft's 'toolbox drawer' and 'map legend' analogies and its generic objectives ('Define classical conditioning using course-appropriate language') are boilerplate, not content.
The draft's claim that classical conditioning is best understood 'as a definition to recite' misrepresents the phenomenon as studied.
